title: Match the grant and token boundary to the client
description: Choose a client, grant, and token location. The lab checks explicit RFC-derived constraints instead of assigning an invented security score.

clients.label: Server-rendered web app
clients.detail: A backend receives the redirect and can protect credentials and tokens from browser JavaScript.
requirements: Use Authorization Code; PKCE with S256 is recommended for confidential web clients
Authenticate the client at the token endpoint with a server-held credential
Keep OAuth tokens on the backend and issue a hardened application session cookie
Register exact HTTPS redirect URIs and bind the transaction to the browser session
clients.refreshGuidance: Store refresh tokens only in the backend token store, bind them to this client, expire inactive grants, and revoke on security events.

clients.label: Single-page application
clients.detail: Browser-delivered JavaScript is a public client; shipped secrets are visible to the user and attackers in the same execution context.
requirements: Use Authorization Code with transaction-specific PKCE S256
Do not register or ship a client secret as proof of SPA identity
Prefer a backend-for-frontend when durable tokens can remain off the browser
If the SPA holds an access token, minimize its lifetime, audience, scope, and exposure
clients.refreshGuidance: Issue a refresh token to a public browser client only after risk assessment; sender-constrain it or use rotation with replay detection.

clients.label: Native mobile or desktop app
clients.detail: Installed binaries are public clients unless each instance receives a separately provisioned credential.
requirements: Use Authorization Code with transaction-specific PKCE S256
Open authorization in an external user-agent rather than an embedded web view
Use app-claimed HTTPS redirects where possible or an allowed native redirect pattern
Treat a secret distributed in the app package as public
clients.refreshGuidance: Keep refresh tokens in platform secure storage and use sender constraint or refresh rotation with family revocation on reuse.

clients.label: Machine-to-machine service
clients.detail: A trusted workload calls an API on its own behalf; no resource owner is present in the grant.
requirements: Use Client Credentials only for a confidential workload acting as itself
Authenticate with a protected secret, private key, or mutual TLS credential
Request a narrow audience and only the scopes the workload needs
Do not represent the resulting subject as an end user
clients.refreshGuidance: A workload can usually authenticate again for a new short-lived access token; a refresh token adds little and increases stored credential risk.

grants.label: Authorization Code + PKCE
grants.detail: A front-channel code is redeemed at the token endpoint with the transaction's verifier.

grants.label: Client Credentials
grants.detail: A confidential workload authenticates and obtains access for itself, without a user grant.

grants.label: Implicit
grants.detail: Returns an access token in the authorization response, increasing leakage and replay exposure.

grants.label: Resource Owner Password
grants.detail: Gives the user's credentials to the client and expands where those credentials can leak.

storage.label: Backend token store
storage.detail: Encrypted server-side storage; the browser receives only a hardened application session cookie.

storage.label: Browser memory
storage.detail: Avoids durable web storage, but malicious script in the same page can still read a live token.

storage.label: Persistent browser storage
storage.detail: Survives reloads and increases the window in which injected script can steal bearer tokens.

storage.label: OS secure storage
storage.detail: Uses the mobile or desktop platform's protected credential facility.

storage.label: Workload secret store
storage.detail: Provides a server workload with protected client credentials and controlled rotation.
